cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: A symmetric distribution has its mean, median, and mode approximately equal; the left and right sides are mirror images.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: Positive (right) skew has a long tail to the right; the mean is greater than the median, which is greater than the mode.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: Negative (left) skew has a long tail to the left; the mean is less than the median, which is less than the mode.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: Pearson's skewness coefficient = 3 × (mean – median) ÷ standard deviation; a positive value indicates positive skew, a negative value indicates negative skew.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: Values of Pearson's skewness coefficient between –0.5 and 0.5 suggest approximately symmetric data; values beyond ±1 indicate substantial skew.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: On a box plot, positive skew is shown by a longer right whisker and the median closer to Q1; negative skew by a longer left whisker and the median closer to Q3.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: Outliers are extreme values that differ significantly from the rest of the data; they can arise from measurement error or genuinely unusual observations.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: The 1.5 × IQR rule: any value below Q1 – 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR is classified as an outlier.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: The 2 standard deviations rule: any value more than 2 standard deviations from the mean may be classified as an outlier, used when the distribution is approximately normal.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: Outliers pull the mean towards them but do not affect the median; this is why the median is preferred for skewed data.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: When deciding whether to include or exclude an outlier, check for data recording errors first; if the value is genuine, analyse the data both with and without the outlier.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Skewness Outliers
cards.back: In exam answers, always identify outliers by showing the calculation (e.g. Q1 – 1.5 × IQR = 10 – 18 = –8) and state whether the outlier should be kept or removed with justification.
